items.stem: An executive asks for a recommendation on a budget decision. Where should the recommendation appear in your communication?

options.text: At the start, with supporting detail following
options.rationale: Correct: leading with the answer (pyramid principle) serves busy decision-makers.
Placing it only at the end makes executives wait through detail first.
An appendix buries the point they asked for.

options.text: Omitted so the audience decides unaided
options.rationale: They asked for a recommendation; omitting it fails the request.

items.explanation: Correct: leading with the answer (pyramid principle) serves busy decision-makers.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which chart choice is a poor fit for comparing many small category shares?

options.text: A pie chart with many thin slices
options.rationale: Correct: many thin pie slices are hard to compare accurately.
A sorted bar chart compares categories clearly.
A table can present many values precisely.
A horizontal bar chart handles many categories well.

items.explanation: Correct: many thin pie slices are hard to compare accurately.

items.stem: Which TWO strengthen an analytics recommendation to executives? (Select TWO)

options.text: State the trade-offs of the recommended option
options.rationale: Correct: trade-offs show the decision was weighed honestly.

options.text: Include how success will be measured
options.rationale: Correct: a measurement plan lets the decision be evaluated later.

options.text: Present only the data with no recommendation
options.rationale: Executives asked for support for a decision, not raw data alone.

options.text: Use maximum chart decoration to look impressive
options.rationale: Decoration (chart junk) distracts from the message.
